question.prompt: What can readers infer about why Ms Whitlock's note mentions muddy conditions, when the class newsletter does not?

stimulus.title: Two Notes About the Excursion
stimulus.body: Text 1 — From the class newsletter: 'Next Tuesday, Year 5 will travel to the Riverside Wildlife Centre. Students must wear full school uniform, bring a labelled water bottle, and arrive at school by 8:15 am sharp, as the bus departs at 8:30 am. Please pack a nut-free lunch, since the centre has a strict allergy policy.' Text 2 — From a note sent home by Ms Whitlock: 'A reminder that our wildlife centre excursion is happening soon. Please make sure your child has closed-in shoes, since parts of the reserve are quite muddy at this time of year, and a labelled water bottle. Morning tea will be provided by the centre, so students do not need to bring their own.'

options.text: As the classroom teacher, she may have more direct, first-hand knowledge of the reserve's current conditions.
The newsletter writer deliberately hid this information from families.
The mud warning is not actually true and was invented by Ms Whitlock.
The wildlife centre changed its conditions after the newsletter was sent.

question.explanation: A classroom teacher writing a personal note may reasonably have more specific, first-hand knowledge or recent updates about site conditions than a general newsletter. There is no evidence in the passage of deliberate concealment or invented information.
